props.title: The Company of Wolves
props.initialSlug: Dark fairy tale twists Red Riding Hood into horror

sections.content: The Company of Wolves (1984) revolutionized fairy tale horror through its feminist reimagining of Little Red Riding Hood. Director Neil Jordan and writer Angela Carter crafted a surreal, psychosexual coming-of-age story that influenced later dark fantasy films like Pan's Labyrinth (2006) and The Shape of Water (2017). The film's striking practical effects - particularly the iconic werewolf transformations where faces peel away to reveal beast beneath - set new standards for practical creature effects, rivaling An American Werewolf in London (1981) for sheer grotesque creativity.

sections.content: The film's layered narrative structure - stories within dreams within stories - influenced later meta-horror like Inception (2010) and The Cabin in the Woods (2012). Jordan's decision to frame everything through young Rosaleen's fever dream allows the film to explore feminine sexuality and power through a uniquely psychological lens. The production design by Anton Furst (who later won an Oscar for Batman (1989)) creates a timeless fairy tale world that feels both ancient and otherworldly.

Carter's involvement in adapting her own short story "The Company of Wolves" helped maintain the feminist themes that would influence later female-centered horror like The VVitch (2015) and Crimson Peak (2015). The film's exploration of sexual awakening through horror imagery created a template for coming-of-age horror that continues in films like Raw (2016) and Ginger Snaps (2000). sections.content: The Company of Wolves sparked renewed interest in adult-oriented fairy tale adaptations, paving the way for films like Brotherhood of the Wolf (2001) and Red Riding Hood (2011). Its blend of practical effects, psychological horror, and feminist themes created a unique sub-genre that continues to influence contemporary filmmakers. The film's emphasis on practical effects over CGI demonstrates how practical creature effects can create a more visceral, dreamlike atmosphere, as later seen in The Thing (1982) and Hellboy (2004).
